turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hello doctor. Thank you for seeing me. You know, it’s a bit funny me being here, because at my age—I’m 87 now, which is just wild to think about sometimes, time really does just fly right by—people always tell you that you're supposed to be slowing down. Most of the folks I know, the ones I went to college with who are still around, they’re perfectly happy to just sit in their recliners and watch the afternoon programs or look out the window. 

But me... well, what brings me in is that, especially for the past year or so, I just feel like I’m always, always doing something. I'm constantly puttering around the house. I'll be fixing a squeaky hinge that barely squeaks, or arranging the pantry, and then rearranging it the very next week because I thought of a better system for the canned goods. And it’s not just at home, I keep volunteering for one more thing at the community center, or taking on baking for the church, even when I know my plate is completely full. I just... I have such a hard time just sitting down and being still. Even at 87! I try to sit on the sofa to rest, and five minutes later I'm up again because I remembered the baseboards need dusting. My daughter keeps telling me I need to learn how to relax and act my age, but I just can't seem to stop moving, it's just go, go, go all day long and I don't really know why I can't just take a breather like everyone else...

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient reports having a hard time sitting down and being still, indicating feelings of restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes being constantly active, stating they are 'always doing something' and that it is 'go, go, go all day long'.

turns.doctor_question: Has this always been the way you’ve been, or is this a change from how you used to be?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you know, it’s funny you ask that, because my daughter was just saying the other day that I’ve suddenly turned into the Energizer Bunny in my old age. But honestly? If I really sit down and think about it—well, when I *do* sit down, which isn't often, as I said—it’s not really new. It’s just that people notice it more now because I’m 87 and supposed to be knitting quietly in a corner. 

But oh my goodness, no, this isn't a new thing at all. It’s been this way my whole life. I mean, going all the way back to when I was just a little girl, long before I even hit my teenage years. I remember being in grade school—this would have been back in the 1940s, mind you, things were very different then, classrooms were very strict and you were expected to just sit perfectly still with your hands folded on the desk. But I just couldn't do it! I was always getting scolded by Mrs. Henderson, my third-grade teacher, because I would just pop right out of my seat. I wouldn't even realize I was doing it half the time, I'd just suddenly be standing up to look out the window or to see what the boy two rows over was drawing. 

And the talking! Oh, my mother used to say I was vaccinated with a phonograph needle. I was always blurting things out, talking right over the other children when I got excited about a topic. They used to tell my parents I was just 'too lively.' That was the word they used back then, 'lively.' They didn't really know what else to call it, but they certainly didn't appreciate it in a classroom setting. So, yes, it's always been there, this bubbling energy. It’s just that now, at my age, people think it’s strange, whereas back then they just thought I was a difficult child who needed to learn some manners. But it’s the exact same feeling, that same urge to just be moving and doing and talking all the time.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes frequently popping out of her seat and standing up during grade school when she was expected to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes herself as rarely sitting down, being compared to the Energizer Bunny, and having a constant urge to be moving and doing things.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient notes she was known for talking constantly, with her mother saying she was 'vaccinated with a phonograph needle.'
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states she was 'always blurting things out.'
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient mentions she would talk right over other children when she got excited.
